extracted.intended_audience: students of English literature, aspiring novelists, and literary critics
extracted.subtask_description: Lecture-style literary-criticism guidance on how to analyze and judge novels by distinct aspects (The Story; People; The Plot; Fantasy; Prophecy; Pattern and Rhythm), with examples and prescriptive remarks about craft and evaluation.

rubrics_metrics.name: The Story
rubrics_metrics.description: The fundamental aspect of the novel: a story is a narrative of events arranged in time sequence; the backbone of a novel.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Primary merit: must make the audience want to know what happens next; primary fault: makes the audience not want to know what happens next. The story narrates the life in time and is indispensable to the novel (no novelist can wholly deny time inside the fabric of his novel). Story-telling devices include suspense (Scheherazade as archetype), ragged ends and incidental episodes, natural introduction of characters, and manipulation of time (Emily Brontë, Sterne, Proust alter or hide clocks but do not abolish time). The story is primitive and oral in quality—it frequently profits from being read aloud and from a recognizable narrative voice. While necessary, story alone is inferior to the 'life by values' and can lead to slack emotion or shallow judgments if relied on exclusively (examples: Sir Walter Scott's strength in story but shallowness of passion; Bennett's The Old Wives' Tale emphasises time; Tolstoy achieves grandeur by combining time with space). Experiments that seek to abolish time (e.g., Gertrude Stein) risk intelligibility and therefore value.

rubrics_metrics.name: Life in Time vs Life by Values
rubrics_metrics.description: A conceptual standard: daily life (and story) obeys chronological sequence ('life in time') but human experience also involves intensity or 'value' that is not measured by chronology ('life by values').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A good novel pays double allegiance: it must include the chronological narrative (the story) and also evoke the life by values (moments of intensity, significance, perception). Devices (to be examined in other aspects) are needed to evoke values alongside time. Purely chronological novels risk celebrating time at the expense of depth; purely value-centered experiments risk unintelligibility. Exemplars: War and Peace combines time with a sense of space to avoid simple depressing decay; Proust and Sterne manipulate chronological order to different effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: People (Characters)
rubrics_metrics.description: The actors of the novel, usually human; characters are invented 'word-masses' roughly describing people and are conditioned by the novelist's temperament.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A novelist's task is to reveal the 'hidden life' (inner thoughts, dreams, joys, sorrows) that history cannot convey; if a character is exactly identical to a real person the work becomes memoir/history. Characters should be plausible humans but distinct from documentary portraiture. The novelist creates characters from imagination but grounded in what he guesses about other people and himself; their nature will be further modified by other aspects of the work (plot, pattern, etc.). The novelist thus must balance verisimilitude with invention and avoid turning fiction into mere historical report.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plot
rubrics_metrics.description: Distinct from story: the plot is an organism of a higher type than the simple time-sequence of events.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The page notes that plot is not the same as story and will be defined in a future lecture; implication for evaluation: look for a higher-order organising principle (causal structure, shape, unity) beyond mere 'and then...and then' narration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fantasy
rubrics_metrics.description: An aspect concerning imaginative or non-realist elements and their execution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The technique of fantasy varies across literary tradition and generations (example: Virginia Woolf’s fantasy resembles Sterne’s in aim but differs in execution and belongs to a later phase of the same tradition). Evaluate fantasy by how it is executed and how it fits the novelist's aims and tradition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prophecy
rubrics_metrics.description: Listed as one of the seven aspects of the novel to be considered.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This aspect is named among the seven focal dimensions but is not elaborated in this chunk; evaluation would address how the novel projects, anticipates, or articulates larger truths or future-directed insight (to be developed in subsequent discussion).

rubrics_metrics.name: Pattern and Rhythm
rubrics_metrics.description: Listed as an aspect of the novel dealing with its formal organisation and cadence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mentioned among the seven aspects (Pattern and Rhythm) but not yet analysed in this lecture excerpt; evaluation should attend to recurring structures, tonal or formal patterns, cadence of prose and larger structural rhythms that produce aesthetic effects beyond plot and character.
